content: In cases of acute asthma, beta₂-agonists are commonly administered via nebulisers to alleviate bronchospasm. However, some experts argue that metered-dose inhalers (MDIs) with holding chambers, also known as spacers, may be equally effective. Nebulisers require an external power source, regular maintenance, and are more costly in community settings compared to spacers. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of spacers versus nebulisers for delivering beta₂-agonists in the treatment of acute asthma. The analysis included randomised trials involving both adults and children (aged two years and older) where spacer-based beta₂-agonist delivery was compared to nebulisation. The data was collected and analysed independently by two reviewers, with missing information obtained directly from study authors or estimated. Results were reported with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The review incorporated data from 39 trials, involving a total of 1897 children and 729 adults. Of these, 33 trials were conducted in emergency room or equivalent community settings, while six trials involved inpatients with acute asthma (207 children and 28 adults). The method of beta₂-agonist delivery—spacer versus nebuliser—did not result in significant differences in hospital admission rates. For adults, the risk ratio (RR) for hospital admission when using spacers compared to nebulisers was 0.94 (95% CI 0.61 to 1.43). For children, the RR was 0.71 (95% CI 0.47 to 1.08), based on moderate-quality evidence. In children, the duration of stay in the emergency department was significantly shorter when spacers were used. On average, children treated with nebulisers spent 103 minutes in the emergency department, whereas those treated with spacers spent 33 minutes less (95% CI -43 to -24 minutes, moderate-quality evidence). For adults, the length of stay in the emergency department was similar regardless of the delivery method. Measures of lung function, such as peak expiratory flow and forced expiratory volume, were comparable between the two delivery methods. However, in children, the use of spacers was associated with a lower pulse rate, with a mean difference of -5% from baseline (95% CI -8% to -2%, moderate-quality evidence). Additionally, the risk of developing tremors was lower with spacers, with a risk ratio of 0.64 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.95, moderate-quality evidence). The authors concluded that nebulisers did not produce significantly better outcomes than MDIs with spacers in either adults or children when treatments were repeated and adjusted based on the patient’s response. Spacers may offer certain advantages for children with acute asthma, such as shorter emergency department stays and fewer side effects like tremors and elevated pulse rates. However, it is important to note that the studies excluded individuals with life-threatening asthma, and therefore, the findings should not be extrapolated to this patient population.
